concepts.heading: Boundaries: Acts of Self-Care, Not Punishment
concepts.plain: A boundary is a way to look after yourself. It is not a way to punish.

concepts.heading: What Boundaries Actually Are
concepts.alt: A guide standing calmly inside a glowing circle drawn on the ground, hand over her heart
concepts.plain: A boundary is a limit you set to keep yourself okay.

concepts.heading: Boundaries vs. Rules
concepts.alt: One points at himself with a thumb while the other wags a finger at someone off to the side
concepts.plain: A boundary is about what you will do. A rule tries to control someone else.

concepts.heading: Why Boundaries Matter in ENM
concepts.alt: A guide juggling three hearts carefully while standing behind a small picket fence
concepts.plain: More relationships means more moments where you need to know your limits.

concepts.heading: Types of Boundaries
concepts.alt: A guide holding four cards showing a hand, a heart, a clock and a speech bubble
concepts.plain: Limits can be about your body, your feelings, your time, your phone or your stuff.

concepts.heading: Reframing Boundaries as Self-Honoring
concepts.alt: A guide hugging herself warmly, a small crown floating above her head
concepts.plain: Each boundary you set tells you that your needs matter.

checks.prompt: "If you stay out late, I will go to bed without waiting up." Is that a boundary or a rule?
checks.explanation: A boundary. A boundary is about what you will do ("I will..."). A rule tells someone else what they must do.

options: A way to control a partner
A limit you set to protect your own wellbeing
checks.explanation: A limit you set to protect your own wellbeing. A boundary is a limit you set to protect your own physical, emotional, or psychological wellbeing.

071377ef-753d-4725-9ecb-f755c07bffac.takeaway: A boundary is about what you will do to look after yourself, not about controlling someone else.

concepts.heading: Marshall Rosenberg's NVC Framework
concepts.plain: NVC is a way to say hard things without blame.

concepts.heading: The Four Steps of NVC
concepts.alt: A guide holding up four fingers beside four stepping stones leading forward
concepts.plain: It has four steps: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you ask.

concepts.heading: 1. Observations (What Happened — Without Judgment)
concepts.alt: A guide looking through a camera lens, a plain photo frame beside her
concepts.plain: Step one: say what happened, just the facts, with no judging.

concepts.heading: 2. Feelings (Emotions, Not Thoughts)
concepts.alt: A guide holding a glowing heart with a small face showing an emotion
concepts.plain: Step two: name the feeling, like sad or scared. Not a thought or a blame.

concepts.heading: 3. Needs (Universal Human Needs)
concepts.alt: A guide holding a battery icon half full next to a heart, a plug in his other hand
concepts.plain: Step three: say the need under the feeling, like trust or rest.

concepts.heading: 4. Requests (Specific, Actionable, Negotiable)
concepts.alt: She offers an open hand with a question mark above it, he considers with a smile
concepts.plain: Step four: ask for one clear thing, and be okay with hearing no.

concepts.heading: NVC in Relationship/Sexual Contexts
concepts.plain: These steps work well for talks about consent, jealousy and sex.

concepts.heading: Common Patterns NVC Replaces
concepts.alt: A guide sweeping broken pointing-finger shapes into a bin with a broom
concepts.plain: It swaps blame, demands and guilt trips for clear, kind words.

checks.prompt: "You came home at midnight." versus "You never care about me." Which one is an observation?
checks.explanation: "You came home at midnight." The first step is to describe what you observed, using concrete, factual language — free from evaluation, interpretation, or blame.

checks.prompt: "Would you be willing to text me if you will be late?" Which NVC step is this?
checks.explanation: A request. Finally, make a clear, specific request — not a demand.

755682e3-d42b-4085-8078-be668b4d08e3.takeaway: Say what happened, how you feel, what you need, and what you are asking for.

concepts.heading: Boundary Challenges Unique to ENM
concepts.plain: Having more than one partner brings limits most couples never have to discuss.

concepts.heading: Time Management Boundaries
concepts.alt: A guide holding a big calendar with coloured hearts on different days
concepts.plain: Time is limited. Be honest about how much you really have to give.

concepts.heading: Sexual Health Agreements
concepts.alt: Each holding a small health checklist card with green ticks, bumping fists
concepts.plain: Be very clear about safer sex, because it affects everyone connected to you.

concepts.heading: Emotional Availability Boundaries
concepts.alt: A guide holding a battery that is nearly empty, a gentle tired smile, hand raised to pause
concepts.plain: Your energy for other people's feelings runs out. It is okay to say so.

concepts.heading: Metamour Boundaries
concepts.alt: Two guides standing a friendly distance apart, a low open gate between them, both waving
concepts.plain: You choose how close you are with your partner's other partners.

concepts.heading: Soft vs. Hard Boundaries
concepts.alt: One hand on a solid brick wall, the other on a swinging garden gate
concepts.plain: A hard limit never bends. A soft limit can shift with trust.

concepts.heading: Using NVC to Communicate Boundary Changes
concepts.plain: Limits change over time. Say so early, using the four steps.

concepts.heading: When a Boundary Is Crossed
concepts.alt: Calmly holding up a hand next to a stepped-on line on the ground
concepts.plain: If someone crosses your limit, name it, say what you need and follow through.

checks.prompt: Sam will never agree to skip barriers with new partners, no matter what. What kind of boundary is that?
checks.explanation: A hard boundary. Not all boundaries carry the same weight: Hard boundaries are non-negotiable.

checks.prompt: "I have no energy left to process this tonight. Can we talk tomorrow?" Which boundary is this?
checks.explanation: Emotional availability. You are a human with finite emotional resources.

1e9e4606-54cc-4c74-8f05-ac7dfefe3a39.takeaway: Know your limits around time, sex and feelings, say them early, and follow through.

concepts.heading: The Art of Receiving Boundaries
concepts.plain: Hearing someone else's "no" well is a skill too.

concepts.heading: Why Receiving Boundaries Is Hard
concepts.alt: A guide holding his chest as small storm clouds swirl around his head
concepts.plain: Someone's limit can sting and feel like rejection. It usually is not about you.

concepts.heading: NVC Empathic Listening
concepts.alt: She speaks while he listens closely, cupping one ear, a heart above them
concepts.plain: Listen to understand. Repeat back what you heard before you react.

concepts.heading: The Difference Between Hearing and Respecting
concepts.alt: A guide bowing slightly with one hand on her heart and the other cupped to her ear
concepts.plain: Hearing a limit is not enough. Respecting it means changing what you do.

concepts.heading: Managing Your Emotional Response
concepts.alt: A guide sitting cross-legged breathing slowly, a small storm cloud shrinking above him
concepts.plain: Name your feeling, breathe, and deal with it without making it their job.

concepts.heading: Asking for Clarification Without Pressuring
concepts.alt: He holds a question mark gently in open palms toward her, she nods
concepts.plain: Ask so you can support them, not so you can talk them out of it.

concepts.heading: Modeling Graceful Acceptance
concepts.plain: When you take a "no" kindly, people feel safe being honest with you.

checks.after: The Difference Between Hearing and Respecting
checks.prompt: Taylor says "I hear you" and then does the thing anyway. What is missing?
checks.explanation: Respecting the boundary. Respecting a boundary means adjusting your behavior accordingly — even when it is inconvenient or emotionally uncomfortable.

checks.prompt: A partner sets a boundary and you are confused. Which reply fits the lesson?
options: "Can you help me understand what you need so I can support that?"
"Why are you doing this to me?"
checks.explanation: "Can you help me understand what you need so I can support that?" There is a difference between.

52aa2645-e6ef-42b5-a58a-aceff9398ed2.takeaway: Taking someone's "no" kindly makes it safe for them to be honest with you.
